items.task: Recall the impact of equity compensation awards on taxable income.
items.stem: Marisol Duran, an employee, holds two stock options. Both were granted at a strike price equal to the stock's value on the grant date, neither has a readily ascertainable fair market value at grant, and both are exercised after they vest. Marisol holds the shares from each exercise for more than two years after grant and more than one year after exercise before selling. Which statement correctly describes the regular income tax results?
options: Both options give compensation income at the grant date equal to the strike price, because the grant is the taxable event
The nonqualified option gives compensation income at exercise equal to the spread, but the incentive option gives none until sale
Neither option produces regular tax income until the shares are sold, and all of the gain on each is taxed as long-term capital gain
The incentive option produces compensation income at exercise, while the nonqualified option is not taxed until the shares are sold
items.rule_line: A nonqualified option is taxed at exercise on the spread; a qualifying incentive stock option has no regular tax at exercise and its sale gain is capital gain.

why.A: Options without a readily ascertainable value are not taxed at grant. Grant is a taxable event only in rare cases where the option itself has a readily ascertainable fair market value.
why.B: A nonqualified option is taxed at exercise on the spread as wages. An incentive stock option that meets the holding requirements is not taxed at exercise for regular tax, and the entire gain on sale is long-term capital gain.
why.C: This is right only for the incentive option. The spread on a nonqualified option is compensation income at exercise, and only later appreciation is capital gain.
why.D: Reverses the two options. The nonqualified option is the one taxed at exercise; the incentive option's spread is an AMT adjustment, not regular income.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Gross income items / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: For each option type, is the spread taxed when exercised or when the shares are sold?
guide.reveal: The nonqualified type is taxed on the spread at exercise as wages; the incentive type is treated differently for regular tax.

guide.ask: With the holding periods met, how is the incentive type's gain taxed on sale?
guide.reveal: Not at exercise for regular tax, and the whole gain is long-term capital gain at sale.

items.task: Recall the impact of equity compensation awards on taxable income.
items.stem: In 2026 Priya Rao, an employee, exercised nonqualified stock options on 1,500 shares at a strike price of $32 per share when the stock's fair market value was $58 per share. She held the shares for 18 months and then sold all of them for $71 per share. What is her long-term capital gain on the sale?
items.rule_line: Basis of stock from a nonqualified option is the strike price plus the spread taxed at exercise; only later appreciation is capital gain.

why.A: The spread at exercise ($39,000) was compensation income, so her basis is the fair market value at exercise, $58 per share. The gain is 1,500 x ($71 - $58) = $19,500.
why.B: This is the compensation income recognized at exercise, not the gain on the later sale.
why.C: Uses the strike price as basis. The spread was already taxed as wages at exercise, so it is added to basis and cannot be taxed again as capital gain.
why.D: Treats the full sale proceeds as gain. Basis is not zero; it is the fair market value at exercise.

steps: Basis per share = fair market value at exercise = $58 (strike $32 + $26 spread taxed as wages)

guide.reveal: Fair market value at exercise, $58 (strike $32 plus the $26 spread already taxed).

items.task: Recall items included in determination and computation of Alternative Minimum Taxable income.
items.stem: In 2026 Ben Ortiz exercised incentive stock options on 2,000 shares at $20 per share when the shares were worth $55 each. He still held all the shares on December 31, 2026. By how much does the exercise increase his 2026 alternative minimum taxable income compared with his regular taxable income?
items.rule_line: The bargain element of an incentive stock option is an AMT adjustment in the year of exercise when the shares are held.

why.A: The spread (2,000 x ($55 - $20) = $70,000) is an AMT adjustment in the year the shares become transferable and not subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture, even though it is not regular income.
why.B: This is the total fair market value of the shares. Only the spread over the exercise price is an adjustment.
why.C: Doubles the total spread, which has no basis in the rule.
why.D: Adds the aggregate exercise price and value.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / AMT / Application

guide.ask: Is an incentive option's spread regular income at exercise, and does it matter for AMT?
guide.reveal: Not regular income, but the spread is an AMT adjustment once the shares are held and vested.

guide.ask: Compute the spread.

items.task: Recall items included in determination and computation of Alternative Minimum Taxable income.
items.stem: Dana Whit, single, itemizes deductions for 2026. Which of the following amounts must be added back to regular taxable income in computing Dana's alternative minimum taxable income?
options: The spread on incentive stock options exercised and still held at year end
Interest on a general obligation bond issued by Dana's home state and held for years
Cash contributions to a public charity that were deducted on Schedule A this year
Qualified interest paid on the acquisition debt of Dana's main home
items.rule_line: Incentive stock option spreads (held at year end) and private activity bond interest increase AMTI; ordinary tax-exempt interest and charitable gifts do not.

why.A: The spread on incentive stock options exercised and held is an AMT adjustment that increases AMTI.
why.B: Interest on ordinary governmental bonds remains excluded for AMT. Only interest on specified private activity bonds is a preference item.
why.C: Charitable contributions are allowed in computing AMTI.
why.D: Interest on acquisition debt for a qualified residence is allowed for AMT.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / AMT / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: Which item is taxed for regular tax only later, or is not deductible in the AMT system?
guide.reveal: Look for the item that is excluded from regular income at exercise but counted for AMT.

guide.ask: Which listed item is that?
guide.reveal: The unsold incentive stock option spread; the deduction and interest items are not added back this way.

items.task: Recall items included in determination and computation of Alternative Minimum Taxable income.
items.stem: Erin Cole, a single taxpayer, has 2026 alternative minimum taxable income of $400,000 before the exemption. Assume her AMT exemption is $90,100 with no phase-out, the AMT rates are 26% on the first $244,500 of AMTI after the exemption and 28% on the excess, and her regular tax liability is $70,000. What is her alternative minimum tax for 2026?
items.rule_line: AMT equals the excess of tentative minimum tax (26% and 28% bands on AMTI less exemption) over regular tax.

why.A: Applies 26% to all AMTI after the exemption and ignores the 28% band above the breakpoint.
why.B: AMTI after exemption = $309,900. Tentative minimum tax = 26% x $244,500 + 28% x $65,400 = $81,882. AMT is the excess over regular tax: $81,882 - $70,000 = $11,882.
why.C: Applies 28% to all AMTI after the exemption instead of using 26% on the first band.
why.D: This is the tentative minimum tax. The AMT is only the excess of tentative minimum tax over regular tax.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / AMT / Application

guide.ask: What AMTI remains after the exemption?
Apply the two rates to the two layers.
How does regular tax enter?
guide.reveal: AMT is only the excess: $81,882 - $70,000 = $11,882.

items.task: Consider the impact to an individual's taxable income for certain items of gross income, including imputed interest on below-market rate loan and compensation earned while employed outside the U.S.
items.stem: On April 1, 2026, Leo Marsh lent his niece $250,000 for use in a business. The loan is payable on demand, bears no interest, and remained outstanding through December 31, 2026. Assume the applicable blended rate for 2026 is 4.0%, and that the below-market gift loan rules are not limited by the borrower's investment income. How much interest income must Leo report for 2026?
items.rule_line: Below-market demand loans have imputed interest at the applicable rate for the period outstanding; a gift loan of $10,000 or less is exempt, and the borrower's net investment income cap applies only to gift loans of $100,000 or less.

why.A: Assumes no income arises when no interest is charged. This gift loan is above the $10,000 exemption and above $100,000, so the investment income cap does not apply and imputed interest income arises.
why.B: Uses the three months before the loan was made (January through March) instead of the nine months it was outstanding.
why.C: A below-market gift loan above $10,000 is not exempt, and above $100,000 the investment income cap does not apply: $250,000 x 4.0% x 9/12 = $7,500 of imputed interest for the period outstanding. Leo reports it as interest income and is treated as making a gift of the same amount.
why.D: Uses a full year of imputed interest. The loan was outstanding for nine months.

items.law_note: Months are used to prorate (9/12); an exact day count would be 275/365. The stem's assumed rate is applied as given.
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Gross income items / Application

guide.ask: Do the exceptions to the below-market loan rules apply to a $250,000 gift loan?
guide.reveal: No; it is over $100,000, so the investment income cap does not limit the imputed interest.

guide.ask: Compute imputed interest for the months outstanding.

items.task: Consider the impact to an individual's taxable income for certain items of gross income, including imputed interest on below-market rate loan and compensation earned while employed outside the U.S.
items.stem: Naomi Pratt, a U.S. citizen, lived and worked in a foreign country for all of 2026 and qualifies for the foreign earned income exclusion under the bona fide residence test. She earned $150,000 from her foreign employer and received $10,000 of interest from a U.S. bank. Assume the 2026 maximum exclusion is $132,900, she elects the exclusion, and she has no foreign housing costs. What amount of gross income does she include on her 2026 return?
items.rule_line: The foreign earned income exclusion removes only foreign earned income, up to the annual dollar limit; other income stays in gross income.

why.A: Excludes all of the wages, as if the exclusion had no dollar limit.
why.B: Excludes the U.S. interest along with the wages. The exclusion applies only to foreign earned income.
why.C: The excludable foreign earned income is the lesser of the exclusion limit and earned income. $150,000 - $132,900 = $17,100 of wages remains, plus $10,000 of interest: $27,100.
why.D: Ignores the foreign earned income exclusion.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Gross income items / Application

guide.ask: How much of her earnings can Naomi exclude?
guide.reveal: The lesser of earned income and the limit, here $132,900.

guide.ask: What is included in gross income?

items.task: Calculate the tax on a child's investment and other unearned income.
items.stem: Owen and Kim Tran's daughter, age 15 and a dependent, has $10,000 of interest income in 2026 and no earned income. Assume her standard deduction is $1,350, the first $2,700 of unearned income is not subject to the parents' rate (the $1,350 not covered by the standard deduction is taxed at her 10% rate), and her parents' marginal rate is 32%. What is her 2026 federal income tax?
items.rule_line: Under the kiddie tax, net unearned income above the threshold is taxed at the parents' rate; the rest of taxable income is taxed at the child's rates.

why.A: Omits the tax at the child's own 10% rate on the first slice of taxable income.
why.B: Net unearned income = $10,000 - $2,700 = $7,300, taxed at 32% = $2,336. The remaining taxable income ($2,700 - $1,350 = $1,350) is taxed at 10% = $135. Total $2,471.
why.C: Taxes all taxable income after the standard deduction at the parents' rate. The first band of unearned income is taxed at the child's rate.
why.D: Taxes all unearned income at the parents' rate and ignores both the standard deduction and the child's own-rate slice.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Kiddie tax / Application

guide.ask: How much of the $10,000 is taxed at the parents' rate?
What remains at her own rate?
guide.reveal: Taxable income left is $2,700 - $1,350 = $1,350, taxed at 10% = $135; total $2,471.

items.task: Calculate the tax on a child's investment and other unearned income.
items.stem: Hana Mori, who is in the 35% bracket, receives $12,000 a year of ordinary interest from bonds and considers giving the bonds to her son, age 12, who has no other income. Assume the son's standard deduction is $1,350, the first $2,700 of his unearned income is not taxed at the parent's rate, and the $1,350 band not covered by the standard deduction is taxed at 10%. Ignoring state tax and the gift tax, what annual federal income tax saving results from the transfer?
items.rule_line: Shifting unearned income to a child saves tax only on the portion below the kiddie tax threshold; income above it is still taxed at the parent's rate.

why.A: Hana now pays $12,000 x 35% = $4,200. After the gift, the son pays 35% on $9,300 of net unearned income ($3,255) plus 10% on $1,350 ($135), or $3,390. Saving = $810.
why.B: Assumes all of the son's taxable income after the standard deduction is taxed at 10%, which overstates the saving.
why.C: This is the son's tax after the transfer, not the saving.
why.D: Treats the son's tax as zero, as if the income escaped tax. Above the threshold the kiddie tax applies the parent's rate.

steps: Tax if Hana keeps the bonds = 12,000 x 35% = $4,200

What does the son pay on the same interest?

items.task: Consider the effect of changing tax rates and legislation on the timing of income and expense items for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Dara Klein, a cash-basis attorney, expects her marginal federal rate to fall from 35% in 2026 to 24% in 2027. She can delay billing $40,000 of fees for December work until January, and she can pay $25,000 of deductible business expenses in December 2026 that she would otherwise pay in January 2027. Ignoring the time value of money and state tax, what federal tax saving results if she takes both actions?
items.rule_line: When rates will fall, defer income and accelerate deductions; each dollar shifted saves the rate difference.

why.A: Subtracts the deduction benefit. Accelerating a deduction into the higher-rate year adds to the saving.
why.B: Counts only the accelerated expenses and omits the income deferral.
why.C: Counts only the income deferral and omits the accelerated deduction.
why.D: Deferring $40,000 of income moves it from the 35% year to the 24% year, saving $4,400. Paying the expenses in 2026 puts the deduction in the 35% year instead of the 24% year, saving $2,750. Total $7,150.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Timing planning / Analysis

guide.ask: What is the rate spread between the two years?
guide.reveal: 35% - 24% = 11 percentage points.

guide.ask: Apply it to the deferred income and the accelerated deduction.

items.task: Consider the effect of changing tax rates and legislation on the timing of income and expense items for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Jun Takeda, a cash-basis freelance designer, finished a client project on December 28, 2026. The client pays within a few days of receiving an invoice. Jun wants the income taxed in 2027. Which action successfully defers the income to 2027?
options: Jun picks up the client's check on December 30 and does not deposit it until January 4
Jun sends the invoice on January 4, 2027, and the client pays after that date
Jun tells the client to leave the check in an unlocked drawer at the client's office, where Jun can collect it at any time
Jun asks the client to transfer the payment to Jun's bank account on December 31 and does not look at the account until January
items.rule_line: A cash-basis taxpayer may delay billing, but income that is paid, credited, or made available without restriction in the year is taxed in that year.

why.A: Receipt of a check in 2026 is receipt of income in 2026. Delaying the deposit does not delay income.
why.B: A cash-basis taxpayer reports income when received or constructively received. Payment that has not been offered or made available in 2026 is not income in 2026.
why.C: Payment that is set apart and available without restriction is constructively received, so it is 2026 income.
why.D: The funds are credited to Jun's account in 2026. Not checking the balance does not defer the income.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Timing planning / Application

guide.ask: When does a cash-basis taxpayer report income?
guide.reveal: When it is actually or constructively received, meaning available without restriction.

guide.ask: Which action leaves payment neither received nor available in 2026?
guide.reveal: Billing after the year ends, so no payment is made or offered in 2026.

items.task: Identify projected tax savings through utilization of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) and qualified health savings accounts (HSAs) for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Tom Reyes, age 43, has family coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan and no other health coverage. He contributes the maximum allowed to a health savings account through payroll deductions under his employer's cafeteria plan. Assume the 2026 family contribution limit is $8,750, his federal marginal rate is 24%, employee-side Social Security and Medicare tax is 7.65%, and state tax is ignored. What is his projected 2026 federal income tax and payroll tax saving?
items.rule_line: HSA contributions made through a cafeteria plan avoid both income tax and FICA; the catch-up amount requires age 55 or older.

why.A: Counts only the payroll tax and omits the income tax saving.
why.B: Counts only income tax. Payroll contributions through a cafeteria plan also reduce FICA wages.
why.C: The contribution reduces income subject to federal tax and, because it runs through the cafeteria plan, FICA wages too. $8,750 x (24% + 7.65%) = $2,769.
why.D: Adds the $1,000 catch-up contribution, which is available only from age 55.

steps: Maximum contribution = 8,750; no catch-up because Tom is under 55
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / FSA/HSA / Application

guide.ask: Does Tom qualify for a catch-up contribution, and what is his contribution?
guide.reveal: No, he is under 55, so the family limit of $8,750 applies.

guide.ask: Which taxes does a cafeteria-plan contribution avoid?
guide.reveal: Both federal income tax and FICA, so $8,750 x (24% + 7.65%) = $2,769.

items.task: Identify projected tax savings through utilization of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) and qualified health savings accounts (HSAs) for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Mia Zhang, age 37, has family coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan through her employer and has no other coverage of her own. Her spouse's employer offers a general-purpose health flexible spending account, and the spouse enrolls in it for 2026 with reimbursement available for the whole family. Which statement about Mia's health savings account for 2026 is correct?
options: Mia may not make HSA contributions because the spouse's general-purpose FSA can reimburse her expenses
Mia may contribute up to the full family limit because the FSA belongs to her spouse and not to her
Mia may contribute the family limit reduced by the amount of the spouse's FSA election
Mia may contribute up to half of the family limit because only her spouse participates in the FSA plan
items.rule_line: A general-purpose health FSA (including a spouse's that covers you) disqualifies HSA contributions; a limited-purpose FSA does not.

why.A: Coverage under a general-purpose health FSA is disqualifying other coverage, even when the FSA belongs to a spouse and covers the family.
why.B: Ownership of the FSA does not matter. Eligibility turns on whether Mia herself can be reimbursed for medical expenses.
why.C: There is no proportional reduction for FSA elections. The FSA coverage either disqualifies her or it does not.
why.D: No half-limit rule exists for this situation. A general-purpose FSA that covers her disqualifies the contribution entirely.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / FSA/HSA / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: What kind of other coverage does a general-purpose health FSA count as?
guide.reveal: Disqualifying other health coverage for HSA purposes.

guide.ask: Does it matter that the FSA is the spouse's?
guide.reveal: No, because it can reimburse Mia's expenses, so it applies to her.

items.task: Consider the impact of using either itemized deductions or the standard deduction for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Ruth and Paul Ochoa file jointly for 2026 with AGI of $200,000 and a 22% marginal rate. The standard deduction is $32,200. Their possible itemized deductions are qualified mortgage interest of $15,000, state income tax of $11,000, real property tax of $8,000, and cash gifts to their church of $6,000. Assume the limitation on state and local taxes is $40,400 for them, and that itemized charitable gifts are deductible only to the extent they exceed 0.5% of AGI. By how much does itemizing reduce their 2026 federal income tax compared with claiming the standard deduction?
items.rule_line: Itemizing helps only by the excess of allowed itemized deductions over the standard deduction, multiplied by the marginal rate.

why.A: Charitable gifts are reduced by 0.5% x $200,000 = $1,000, leaving $5,000. Itemized deductions = $39,000, which exceeds the standard deduction by $6,800. Tax saving = $6,800 x 22% = $1,496.
why.B: Ignores the 0.5% of AGI floor on charitable gifts.
why.C: Reports the extra deduction instead of the tax it saves.
why.D: Applies the rate to the whole itemized total instead of only the excess over the standard deduction they would receive anyway.

steps: Itemized total = 15,000 + 19,000 (state and local taxes, under the limit) + $5,000 = $39,000
items.law_note: P.L. 119-21 §70425 added the 0.5%-of-contribution-base floor on itemized charitable deductions for tax years beginning after 2025; SALT limit and threshold are supplied in the stem.

items.task: Consider the impact of using either itemized deductions or the standard deduction for planning purposes given a specific scenario.
items.stem: Amir and Sana Haddad file jointly, have AGI of $150,000 in both 2026 and 2027, and a 22% marginal rate. Each year they have $22,000 of mortgage interest and state and local taxes combined, and they normally give $8,000 in cash to charity. The standard deduction is $32,200 each year, and itemized charitable gifts are deductible only to the extent they exceed 0.5% of AGI. They consider giving $16,000 to a donor-advised fund in 2026 and nothing in 2027, claiming the larger deduction in whichever year is better. What is the two-year federal tax saving from bunching?
items.rule_line: Bunching pays when itemized deductions alternate above and below the standard deduction; the floor applies once to the bunched gift.

why.A: Without bunching each year's itemized total ($29,250) is below the standard deduction, so they deduct $64,400 over two years. With bunching, 2026 itemized deductions are $37,250 and 2027 uses the standard deduction of $32,200, for $69,450. The extra $5,050 x 22% = $1,111.
why.B: Ignores the 0.5% of AGI floor on the bunched gift.
why.C: Applies the rate to the whole gift. Without bunching the standard deduction already gives them part of that benefit, so only the added deduction counts.
why.D: Reports the added deductions instead of the tax saving.

steps: No bunching: max($29,250, 32,200) = 32,200 each year, total $64,400

items.task: Calculate estimated tax payments required for an individual to avoid underpayment penalties given a specific planning scenario.
items.stem: Jenna Brandt, a single taxpayer, had 2025 AGI of $165,000 and total 2025 tax of $38,000. She expects her 2026 total tax to be $52,000. Her employer will withhold $10,000 for the year, spread evenly, and she wants to make four equal estimated payments that are just enough to avoid the underpayment penalty. What is each payment?
items.rule_line: To avoid the penalty pay the smaller of 90% of current-year tax or 100% (110% if prior AGI exceeds $150,000) of prior-year tax, less withholding.

why.A: Uses 100% of prior-year tax. With prior-year AGI above $150,000 the prior-year safe harbor is 110%.
why.B: Her prior-year AGI exceeds $150,000, so the prior-year safe harbor is 110% of 2025 tax = $41,800. The current-year safe harbor is 90% of $52,000 = $46,800. The smaller, $41,800, less withholding of $10,000 leaves $31,800, or $7,950 per installment.
why.C: Uses only the 90% current-year test. The smaller of the two safe harbors is enough to avoid the penalty.
why.D: Pays 100% of the expected current-year tax. That is more than the law requires.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Estimated tax / Application

guide.ask: Which prior-year safe harbor percentage applies when 2025 AGI is above $150,000?
Compare with the current-year test and pick the smaller.
guide.reveal: 90% x $52,000 = $46,800, so the required payment is $41,800.

guide.ask: Subtract withholding and divide.

items.task: Calculate estimated tax payments required for an individual to avoid underpayment penalties given a specific planning scenario.
items.stem: Andre Silva is a salaried employee with no other income. He made no estimated tax payments in 2026, and in early December he learns that his withholding will fall far short of the amount needed to avoid the underpayment penalty. His employer will still process payroll for the rest of December. Which action best reduces the penalty for the year?
options: Mail a single large estimated tax payment on December 31 to cover the full shortfall for the year
Submit a new Form W-4 asking the employer to increase withholding on remaining pay
Wait to file the return and pay the balance due by April 15 of the following year
File Form 4868 to extend the time to file the return, and pay the balance with it
items.rule_line: Withholding is deemed paid evenly over the year, so late-year withholding increases can eliminate earlier installment shortfalls; estimated payments count when made.

why.A: An estimated payment counts only from the date it is paid. The earlier installments remain underpaid and still bear the penalty.
why.B: Withholding is treated as paid in equal installments on the due dates regardless of when it is actually withheld, so extra withholding late in the year cures earlier shortfalls.
why.C: The penalty is computed for each installment due date, so paying with the return does not remove the penalty already accrued.
why.D: An extension to file does not extend the time to pay, and the penalty is unaffected.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Estimated tax / Application

guide.ask: How does the penalty test treat tax withheld during the year?
guide.reveal: Withholding is treated as if paid evenly over the year, regardless of when it was actually withheld.

items.task: Calculate estimated tax payments required for an individual to avoid underpayment penalties given a specific planning scenario.
items.stem: Padma Iyer, a U.S. citizen, had no federal income tax liability for 2025, a full 12-month tax year, because of a large business loss. In 2026 she earns substantial income and expects a total tax of $30,000. She had no withholding and made no estimated payments during 2026. Which statement about the underpayment of estimated tax penalty for 2026 is correct?
options: A penalty applies to the entire $30,000 because she paid less than 90% of her 2026 tax liability
A penalty applies only to the installments due after she first receives the income
No penalty applies only if she pays at least half of the $30,000 by September 15
No penalty applies, because she owed no tax for 2025 and it was a full 12-month year
items.rule_line: No estimated tax penalty applies if the prior year was a 12-month year with zero tax liability and the taxpayer was a citizen or resident all year.

why.A: The 90% test is only one way to avoid the penalty. An exception applies when the prior-year liability was zero.
why.B: That describes the annualized income installment method, which does not need to be used here because no penalty is imposed at all.
why.C: There is no half-of-tax test. The exception is automatic when the prior-year tax was zero.
why.D: A taxpayer who owed no tax for a 12-month prior year, and was a citizen or resident throughout it, has no estimated tax penalty for the current year.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group A / Estimated tax / Application

guide.ask: What special exception exists based on the prior year?
guide.reveal: No penalty if the prior year was a full 12-month year and she owed no tax, as a citizen or resident.

guide.ask: Do her 2025 facts meet it?
guide.reveal: Yes, she owed no 2025 tax for a 12-month year, so her 2026 income does not create a penalty.

items.stem: Grace Lindqvist, who is in the 35% bracket and pays 15% on long-term capital gains, wants to give $40,000 to her public charity. She owns stock worth $40,000 with a basis of $10,000 that she has held for three years. She could either (1) give the stock, or (2) sell it and give the after-tax proceeds in cash. Assume all deductions are fully allowed within the AGI limits and ignore state tax and the net investment income tax. How much larger is her net federal tax benefit (charitable deduction saving minus any capital gains tax) from the stock gift than from the cash gift?
items.rule_line: Donating long-term appreciated stock to a public charity avoids the gain and allows a deduction at fair market value; selling first loses both benefits.

why.A: This is only the extra deduction value ($4,500 x 35%) from giving the full $40,000 instead of $35,500. It leaves out the $4,500 capital gains tax that selling triggers.
why.B: Counts only the capital gains tax avoided and ignores the larger charitable deduction.
why.C: Giving the stock avoids the $4,500 capital gains tax and yields a deduction of $40,000 x 35% = $14,000. Selling first leaves $35,500 of cash to give, a deduction worth $12,425, and costs $4,500 of tax, for a net $7,925. The difference is $6,075.
why.D: Treats the whole deduction as the advantage. The cash gift also produces a deduction, so only the difference counts.

steps: Stock gift: deduction 40,000 x 35% = $14,000; no gain tax
Sale first: tax $4,500; cash gift $35,500 x 35% = $12,425; net $7,925

Jim recognizes a $70,000 gain, and his former spouse takes a basis of $90,000
Jim recognizes no gain, and his former spouse takes a $90,000 stepped-up basis

why.D: The one-year period is a safe harbor, and transfers made within six years under the divorce instrument are also covered.

items.stem: Ted Wilkes sold his entire interest in a rental activity to an unrelated buyer in 2026 in a fully taxable sale. The activity had a current-year passive loss of $6,000 before the sale, $40,000 of suspended passive losses from earlier years, and Ted's gain on the sale was $25,000. He has no other passive items. By what net amount does the activity reduce his 2026 adjusted gross income?
items.rule_line: A fully taxable disposition of a passive activity to an unrelated party frees all suspended losses to offset the gain and then other income.

why.A: Allows only the current loss and leaves suspended losses suspended. A full taxable disposition releases them.
why.B: Forgets the current-year loss of the activity, which is also deductible.
why.C: On a fully taxable disposition of the entire interest all losses are released. The activity's net effect is the gain of $25,000 less the current loss of $6,000 and the suspended losses of $40,000: $21,000 reduction in AGI.
why.D: Leaves out the gain on the sale, which offsets the losses.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / Suspended losses / Application

guide.ask: Does a fully taxable sale of the entire interest release the suspended losses?
guide.reveal: Yes, all suspended and current losses become deductible.

guide.ask: Net the losses against the gain.
guide.reveal: $6,000 + $40,000 = $46,000 of losses less $25,000 of gain reduces AGI by $21,000.

items.task: Calculate utilization of suspended losses on the disposition of a passive activity for tax purposes.
items.stem: Rhea Colton owns a rental property with $30,000 of suspended passive losses. The property has a fair market value of $200,000 and an adjusted basis of $120,000. She gives her entire interest to her son in 2026. Which statement about the suspended losses is correct?
options: Rhea deducts the suspended losses in 2026 because she has disposed of her entire interest in the activity
Rhea's son inherits the suspended losses and may deduct them against his passive income from other activities
Rhea deducts the suspended losses up to the $80,000 built-in gain, and any excess is added to the son's basis
Rhea cannot deduct the suspended losses, and her son's basis in the property is increased by them
items.rule_line: A gift of a passive activity does not release suspended losses; they increase the donee's basis.

why.A: The release of suspended losses requires a fully taxable disposition. A gift is not taxable.
why.B: Suspended losses do not carry over to the donee as passive losses; they become part of his basis.
why.C: No deduction is available on a gift. The gain limitation is not a rule for these losses.
why.D: A gift is not a taxable disposition. The suspended losses are not deductible by the donor; they are added to the donee's basis instead.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / Suspended losses / Application

guide.ask: Is a gift of the property a taxable disposition that frees suspended losses?
guide.reveal: No, a gift does not free them for the donor.

guide.ask: Where do the suspended losses go instead?
guide.reveal: They are added to the donee's basis, so the son's basis rises.

items.stem: Four taxpayers each materially participate in their rental real estate and want to treat their rentals as nonpassive as real estate professionals in 2026. Which taxpayer meets the personal service tests?
options: Ben, who spent 1,100 hours in real property businesses and 800 hours as an employee of an unrelated company
Anna, who spent 900 hours in real property businesses and 1,000 hours as an employee of an unrelated company
Cara, who spent 700 hours in real property businesses and held no other job at any time during the year
Dev, who spent 800 hours in real property businesses and 800 hours as an employee of an unrelated company
items.rule_line: A real estate professional must spend more than 750 hours in real property trades or businesses and more than half of all personal service hours there.

why.A: More than half of his personal service time (1,100 of 1,900 hours) is in real property businesses, and the total exceeds 750 hours.
why.B: Real property time (900 of 1,900 hours) is less than half of her total personal service time.
why.C: Her share of time is 100%, but she has fewer than 750 hours in real property businesses.
why.D: Exactly half is not enough. The real property time must be more than half of all personal service time.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / Passive activity loss / Application

guide.ask: What two tests must a real estate professional meet?
guide.reveal: More than half of personal service time in real property businesses, and more than 750 hours in them.

guide.ask: Which person meets both?
guide.reveal: Compare each real property share with total hours, and check the 750 threshold.

items.task: Calculate the at-risk loss limitation for an activity in which an individual materially participates, including losses from pass-through entities and losses from real estate rental activities with active participation.
items.stem: Nisha Shah is a limited partner (a passive activity for her). Her share of the partnership's 2026 loss is $80,000. Her outside basis at year end before the loss is $60,000, her at-risk amount is $45,000, and she has $20,000 of passive income from another partnership. She has no other passive items. How much of the loss is suspended because of the passive activity rules, after the basis and at-risk limits have been applied?
items.rule_line: Partnership losses pass three limits in order: basis, at-risk, then passive activity; each disallowed piece is carried forward.

why.A: This is the part suspended by the at-risk limit, not the passive activity limit.
why.B: This is the part suspended by the basis limit, not the passive activity limit.
why.C: The limits apply in order: basis ($60,000), then at-risk ($45,000), then the passive activity rules. After the first two, $45,000 remains, and the passive rules allow a deduction only against $20,000 of passive income. The amount suspended by the passive rules is $45,000 - $20,000 = $25,000.
why.D: Applies the passive limit to the entire loss and ignores the basis and at-risk limits applied first.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / At-risk limitation / Analysis

guide.ask: In what order are the limits applied?
guide.reveal: Basis first, then at-risk, then passive activity rules.

guide.ask: What amount remains after the first two, and how much can offset passive income?
guide.reveal: $45,000 remains after basis and at-risk, of which $20,000 can be used, so $25,000 is suspended by the passive rules.

items.stem: Which statement about the at-risk rules for an individual investor is correct?
options: Any nonrecourse debt on the activity increases the amount at risk when it is secured by the taxpayer's other property
An amount borrowed for the activity from a person who has an interest in the activity, other than as a creditor, is not treated as at risk
The at-risk limitation is applied after the passive activity loss rules, and any loss allowed by the passive rules is at risk by definition
The at-risk limitation applies only to activities that are passive for the taxpayer
items.rule_line: At-risk excludes nonrecourse debt (except qualified real estate financing) and loans from interested persons; it applies before the passive activity rules.

why.A: Nonrecourse debt is generally not at risk. The exception is qualified nonrecourse financing on real property from an unrelated lender.
why.B: Loans from an owner or a related party with an interest in the activity are excluded from the amount at risk.
why.C: The at-risk rules are applied before the passive activity rules, after basis.
why.D: The limitation applies to most trade, business and investment activities, whether passive or not.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / At-risk limitation / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: Which loans are excluded from at-risk amounts?
guide.reveal: Borrowings from a person with an interest in the activity other than as a creditor.

guide.ask: Which statement matches that rule?
guide.reveal: The one about amounts borrowed from an interested owner; the other statements misstate the order or the scope of the rules.

items.stem: Xavier and Yara each have an outside basis and at-risk amount large enough to deduct a $50,000 loss from a partnership in 2026 and otherwise have identical incomes. Xavier is a general partner who works full time in the partnership's business. Yara is a limited partner who does not participate, and she has $10,000 of passive income from another investment. By how much more does the loss reduce Xavier's taxable income than it reduces Yara's?
items.rule_line: A nonpassive loss offsets all income; a passive loss offsets only passive income.

why.A: This is Yara's benefit, not the difference between the two.
why.B: Doubles Yara's offset against passive income.
why.C: Subtracts Yara's passive income twice.
why.D: Xavier's loss is nonpassive and reduces his taxable income by $50,000. Yara's loss is passive and is deductible only against her $10,000 of passive income, so it reduces her taxable income by $10,000. The difference is $40,000.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group B / Passive activity loss / Application

guide.ask: How is Xavier's loss classified?
guide.reveal: Nonpassive, since he works full time in the business, so all $50,000 offsets other income.

guide.ask: How much of Yara's loss can she deduct, and what is the gap?
guide.reveal: Passive, limited to her $10,000 of passive income, so the difference is $50,000 - $10,000 = $40,000.

items.stem: Beth Nolan wants to help her grandson, who is not her dependent, with college costs in 2026. Which payment is excluded from gift tax without using her annual exclusion or filing a gift tax return?
options: A payment of the same tuition amount made to her grandson, who then pays the college
A payment of the grandson's room and board made directly to the college
A payment of tuition made directly to the college for her grandson
A payment of the tuition made to the grandson's parents, who then pay the college
items.rule_line: Direct payments of tuition to a school, or medical costs to a provider, are excluded from gift tax without limit.

why.A: The unlimited exclusion applies only to payments made directly to the institution. A payment to the grandson is a gift eligible for the annual exclusion.
why.B: The exclusion covers tuition only, not room and board, books or supplies.
why.C: Tuition paid directly to the educational institution is excluded from taxable gifts regardless of amount and does not use the annual exclusion.
why.D: A payment to the parents is a gift to them. Only direct payments to the school qualify.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Gift tax deductions/exclusions / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: Which payments to a school are excluded regardless of amount?
guide.reveal: Tuition paid directly to the educational institution.

guide.ask: Which choice matches this?
guide.reveal: The one where the payer sends the tuition directly to the college, not through family members.

items.task: Explain the unified transfer tax system and how the annual exclusion, marital deduction and the unified credit impact the planning for gifts and gift taxation.
items.stem: Which statement about the federal gift tax annual exclusion and marital deduction is correct for 2026?
options: Gifts of a future interest in a trust qualify for the annual exclusion if the trust is irrevocable and long-term
Gifts of any amount to a spouse who is not a U.S. citizen qualify for the unlimited marital deduction
The annual exclusion is a single lifetime cap that is gradually used up as the donor makes gifts of any kind
Each donee may receive a present-interest gift up to the annual exclusion, and outright gifts to a citizen spouse are deductible
items.rule_line: The annual exclusion is per donee per year for present interests; the marital deduction is unlimited for a citizen spouse.

why.A: A future interest does not qualify for the annual exclusion unless the beneficiary has a present right to use or enjoy the property.
why.B: For a noncitizen spouse the marital deduction is replaced by a dollar-limited annual exclusion.
why.C: The annual exclusion is available each year per donee. The unified credit is the cumulative amount.
why.D: The annual exclusion is per donee for present interests, and the unlimited marital deduction applies to outright gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Unified transfer tax system / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: What is the annual exclusion per donee limited to?
guide.reveal: Present-interest gifts only, per donee each year, not a lifetime cap.

guide.ask: What about gifts to a spouse?
guide.reveal: Outright gifts to a U.S. citizen spouse qualify for the unlimited marital deduction.

The annual exclusion is $19,000 per donee. What are his total taxable gifts for 2026?

why.A: The direct tuition payment is excluded and the gift to his wife qualifies for the marital deduction. The taxable gifts are ($80,000 - $19,000) + ($30,000 - $19,000) = $72,000.
why.B: Treats the tuition payment as a gift eligible for the annual exclusion. Direct tuition payments are excluded entirely.
why.C: Ignores the annual exclusion for each donee.
why.D: Includes the gift to his wife. Gifts to a citizen spouse qualify for the unlimited marital deduction.

steps: Tuition paid directly: excluded; spouse gift: marital deduction

items.rule_line: Gift tax is computed on cumulative taxable gifts, reduced by the unified credit equal to tax on the basic exclusion amount.

why.A: Cumulative taxable gifts are $9,000,000 + $6,900,000 = $15,900,000. The excess over the $15,000,000 exclusion is $900,000, taxed at 40%: $360,000.
why.B: Reports the excess over the exclusion without applying the 40% rate.
why.C: Taxes the 2026 gifts alone and ignores the exclusion already used against prior gifts and the amount still unused.
why.D: Taxes cumulative gifts without allowing the exclusion.

items.stem: Frank Duarte, age 82 and in poor health, owns stock worth $100,000 with a basis of $20,000. His estate is well below the federal estate tax exemption. He can give the stock to his daughter now or leave it to her in his will, and she plans to sell it soon after receiving it. Her long-term capital gains rate is 20%, and the value will not change. How much less federal income tax does she pay if she inherits the stock instead of receiving it as a gift?
items.rule_line: Property held until death gets a stepped-up basis; a lifetime gift carries over the donor's basis.

why.A: Applies the rate to the basis, not to the built-in gain.
why.B: Applies a 10% rate instead of the 20% rate.
why.C: Applies a 15% rate instead of the 20% rate.
why.D: A donee takes the donor's basis ($20,000), so a sale produces $80,000 of gain. An heir's basis is stepped up to fair market value at death ($100,000), so the sale produces no gain. The saving is $80,000 x 20% = $16,000.

steps: Bequest: basis = fair market value, gain = 0
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Gifting for planning / Analysis

guide.ask: What basis does the daughter take in a gift versus an inheritance?
guide.reveal: Gift: the donor's basis of $20,000. Inheritance: fair market value at death, $100,000.

guide.ask: Compute the difference in tax.
guide.reveal: Gain of $80,000 under a gift, none under a bequest; $80,000 x 20% = $16,000.

items.stem: Paul Stein gave his niece stock with a fair market value of $130,000 and an adjusted basis to him of $65,000. He paid $18,000 of gift tax on the gift. The annual exclusion was $19,000. What is his niece's basis in the stock for computing gain?
items.rule_line: The donee's basis increases by the gift tax paid multiplied by the ratio of net appreciation to the amount of the gift.

why.A: Uses only the donor's basis. The gift tax paid on appreciation is added to basis.
why.B: Computes the appreciation share against the full fair market value instead of the value net of the annual exclusion.
why.C: The niece's basis is the donor's basis plus the part of the gift tax attributable to net appreciation: $18,000 x ($65,000 / $111,000) = $10,541. Basis = $65,000 + $10,541 = $75,541.
why.D: Adds all of the gift tax to basis. Only the part attributable to appreciation is added.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group C / Gifting for planning / Application

guide.ask: What is the starting basis for the niece?
guide.reveal: The donor's basis of $65,000.

guide.ask: How much of the gift tax is added?
guide.reveal: $18,000 x $65,000 / $111,000 = $10,541, where $111,000 is the gift less the exclusion. Basis = $75,541.

why.B: Each gift is within the annual exclusion, so no return is required.

why.D: A direct tuition payment is excluded, and no return is required.

items.stem: Nolan and Iris Berg, a married couple, want to contribute a lump sum to a 529 plan for their grandson in 2026 without using any lifetime exemption and without paying gift tax. They elect to treat the contribution as made evenly over five years and to split gifts. The annual exclusion is $19,000 per donor per donee. What is the largest lump sum they can contribute?
items.rule_line: A 529 contribution may be averaged over five years of annual exclusions per donor; splitting doubles it for a married couple.

why.A: Applies only one year's exclusion for each spouse. The five-year election allows five years' worth.
why.B: Allows five years of exclusion for one spouse only. Gift splitting allows both spouses' exclusions.
why.C: Each spouse may use five years of the annual exclusion in one year: $19,000 x 5 = $95,000. With gift splitting the two spouses together can contribute $190,000.
why.D: Doubles the amount again. Two spouses are the only donors.

items.stem: Ellen Ross, age 62, opened a Roth IRA eight years ago, made only after-tax contributions, and in 2026 withdraws the entire account balance, which includes investment earnings. Which statement about the distribution is correct?
options: The earnings are ordinary income and subject to the 10% additional tax because she took the entire balance
It is a qualified distribution, so neither her contributions nor the earnings are included in gross income
The earnings are ordinary income, but the 10% additional tax does not apply because she is over 59 1/2
The earnings are excluded only to the extent the funds are used for a first-time home purchase
items.rule_line: A Roth IRA distribution is qualified, and tax-free, after a five-year period if the owner is 59 1/2 or older, disabled, or has died, or for a first-home purchase.

why.A: The additional tax applies to nonqualified distributions before age 59 1/2. This distribution is qualified.
why.B: A Roth distribution after age 59 1/2 and after the five-year holding period is qualified, so the earnings are excluded along with the contributions.
why.C: This mixes the rules. The five-year period and age test are both met, so the earnings are not taxed either.
why.D: The first-home rule is a separate exception for early distributions. It is not needed for a qualified distribution.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group D / Retirement plans / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: Does Ellen meet the age and five-year requirements for a Roth distribution?
guide.reveal: Yes, she is over 59 1/2 and the account is eight years old.

guide.ask: What does that make the distribution?
guide.reveal: A qualified one, so neither contributions nor earnings are in gross income and no additional tax applies.

items.stem: Rosa Vidal, age 63, paid $100,000 for a nonqualified deferred annuity contract that is now worth $130,000. She withdraws $20,000 in 2026 without annuitizing the contract. How much of the withdrawal is included in her gross income?
items.rule_line: Partial withdrawals from a nonqualified deferred annuity are taxed as earnings first, up to the total gain in the contract.

why.A: Applies a pro rata basis recovery. Withdrawals before annuitization come out earnings first.
why.B: Withdrawals from a nonqualified deferred annuity before annuitization are treated as earnings first (last-in, first-out). Earnings are $130,000 - $100,000 = $30,000, which exceeds the $20,000 withdrawal, so the entire withdrawal is taxable.
why.C: Includes all of the contract's earnings even though only a part was withdrawn.
why.D: Reports the value of the contract as income.

steps: Taxable = lesser of withdrawal 20,000 and gain $30,000 = $20,000
items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group D / Retirement plans / Application

guide.ask: In what order does a nonqualified deferred annuity pay out before annuitization?
guide.reveal: Earnings come out first, then the investment in the contract.

guide.ask: Compare the gain with the withdrawal.
guide.reveal: The gain is $130,000 - $100,000 = $30,000, more than $20,000, so the whole withdrawal is taxable.

items.stem: Amy Kwon, age 44, has one traditional IRA holding $90,000, of which $9,000 is from nondeductible contributions she made in earlier years. She has no other IRAs. In 2026 she converts $30,000 of the IRA to a Roth IRA. Assume the total IRA balance at year end, counting the amount converted, is still $90,000. How much of the conversion is included in her gross income?
items.rule_line: Distributions and conversions from traditional IRAs with basis are taxable in proportion to pre-tax dollars in all IRAs.

why.A: Computes the nontaxable part instead of the taxable part.
why.B: Subtracts all of the basis from the amount converted. Basis is recovered in proportion to the whole IRA balance, not first.
why.C: The pro rata rule treats each distribution as part taxable and part basis: the nontaxable fraction is $9,000/$90,000 = 10%. The taxable amount is $30,000 x 90% = $27,000.
why.D: Ignores the nondeductible basis.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group D / Retirement plans / Application

items.stem: Pat Simon has $7,000 of pre-tax earnings available to save and expects the money to double before retirement. Pat's marginal rate is 24% now and is expected to be 32% in retirement. Under the traditional IRA choice Pat deducts a $7,000 contribution and pays tax on the withdrawal. Under the Roth IRA choice Pat pays tax on the $7,000 first and contributes the rest. Ignoring all other rules, which choice leaves more after tax at retirement, and by how much?
options: The traditional IRA, by $1,120
The Roth IRA, by $2,800
The Roth IRA, by $1,120
The two choices leave the same amount after tax
items.rule_line: When the retirement rate exceeds the current rate, paying tax now through a Roth increases the after-tax amount; equal rates give equal results.

why.A: Reverses the comparison. The higher rate at retirement favors paying tax now.
why.B: Compares the tax paid in nominal dollars (retirement tax against tax now) instead of comparing after-tax accumulations.
why.C: Traditional: $7,000 doubles to $14,000 and is taxed at 32%, leaving $9,520. Roth: $7,000 less 24% tax leaves $5,320, which doubles to $10,640 tax-free. The Roth leaves $1,120 more.
why.D: This holds only if the rate at retirement equals the rate now, which is not the case here.

guide.ask: What does the Roth path leave?
Compare.
guide.reveal: $10,640 - $9,520 = $1,120 in favor of the Roth.

The uniform lifetime table factors are 26.5 at age 73, 25.5 at age 74 and 24.6 at age 75. What is his required minimum distribution for 2026?
items.rule_line: The RMD equals the prior December 31 account balance divided by the uniform lifetime factor for the age attained during the year.

why.A: Uses the age 73 factor. The factor is for the age reached in 2026.
why.B: The 2026 distribution uses the prior year-end balance and the factor for his age at the end of 2026 (74): $1,000,000 / 25.5 = $39,216.
why.C: Uses the age 75 factor.
why.D: Uses the December 31, 2026 balance. The required distribution is based on the prior year-end balance.

She used $10,000 of it to buy her first home under the rules for first-time homebuyers, and spent the remaining $10,000 on a vacation. Her marginal rate is 24%. What is the total of her federal income tax and additional tax on the early distribution?
items.rule_line: Early IRA distributions are taxable; the 10% additional tax is waived on up to $10,000 used for a first home.

why.A: Counts only the additional tax and omits the income tax.
why.B: Omits the 10% additional tax on the part that does not qualify for the exception.
why.C: The whole withdrawal is taxable: $20,000 x 24% = $4,800. The 10% additional tax applies only to the $10,000 that does not qualify for the first-time homebuyer exception: $1,000. Total $5,800.
why.D: Applies the additional tax to the whole withdrawal. The first-home exception covers up to $10,000.

items.task: Demonstrate an understanding of the risks associated with different investment options, including equity securities, corporate bonds and municipal bonds.
items.stem: Which statement about investment risk is correct?
options: Long-term fixed-rate bonds are less sensitive to changes in interest rates than short-term fixed-rate bonds
Interest on a municipal bond is exempt from federal income tax, so the bond carries no risk of default
An investment-grade corporate bond carries no market price risk if it is held to maturity
Holding shares of many unrelated companies reduces company-specific risk but does not eliminate market risk
items.rule_line: Diversification reduces company-specific risk; interest rate, credit, and market risks remain for bonds and stocks.

why.A: The reverse is true: longer maturities have larger price changes when rates change.
why.B: Tax exemption of the interest has no effect on the issuer's ability to pay. Municipal bonds carry credit risk.
why.C: Holding to maturity avoids realizing a price loss, but the bond still carries interest rate and credit risk during the holding period.
why.D: Diversification removes risk that is unique to an issuer. Risk that affects the whole market remains.

items.blueprint_tag: TCP Area I / Group D / Investment risk / Remembering & Understanding

guide.ask: Which risks can be diversified away and which cannot?
guide.reveal: Risk specific to one issuer can be diversified away, but risk that affects the whole market cannot.

guide.reveal: The one about holding many unrelated companies.

items.stem: Gina Frost, whose federal marginal rate on ordinary income is 35%, is choosing between a corporate bond and a state municipal bond. items.rule_line: After-tax yield equals the pre-tax yield multiplied by one minus the total tax rate, including the net investment income tax where it applies.

why.A: Interest is taxed at 35% plus 3.8%: 5.6% x (1 - 0.35 - 0.038) = 3.43%.
why.B: Omits the 3.8% net investment income tax.
why.C: Applies only the net investment income tax and omits the income tax.
why.D: Computes a tax-equivalent yield, which grosses up a tax-free yield, instead of reducing the taxable yield.

items.rule_line: A scholarship is excluded to the extent it pays tuition, required fees, and required books, supplies and equipment; room and board is taxable.

why.B: Amounts used for tuition, required fees and required books are excluded. The $2,000 used for room and board is included in income.

items.task: Explain how insurance is used in planning to mitigate risk, including life insurance, long-term care insurance and umbrella policies.
items.stem: Carl Price owned a life insurance policy on his own life and named his daughter as the beneficiary. He died in 2026 while still owning the policy. Which statement about the death benefit is correct?
options: It is included in the daughter's gross income as ordinary income and excluded from Carl's gross estate
It is excluded from the daughter's gross income and included in Carl's gross estate
It is excluded from the daughter's gross income and excluded from Carl's gross estate because it passed by beneficiary designation
It is included in the daughter's gross income to the extent it exceeds the premiums Carl paid
items.rule_line: Life insurance proceeds are excluded from the beneficiary's income and are included in the estate when the insured had incidents of ownership.

why.A: Death benefits are excluded from the beneficiary's income, and a policy the insured owned is part of the estate.
why.B: Death benefits paid by reason of the insured's death are excluded from income, and proceeds of a policy owned by the insured are included in the estate.
why.C: Naming a beneficiary does not keep the proceeds out of the estate when the insured owned the policy.
why.D: The excess over premiums is excluded from income when paid by reason of death.

guide.ask: Is life insurance paid at death taxed to the beneficiary as income?
guide.reveal: No, death benefits are generally excluded from the recipient's income.

guide.ask: What about the insured's estate when the insured owned the policy?
guide.reveal: The proceeds are included in the gross estate.

items.task: Demonstrate an understanding of the implications of legal ownership of an asset and beneficiary designations on an estate and its beneficiaries.
items.stem: Dora Eaton's will leaves all of her property to her son. At her death, her 401(k) account named her daughter as the sole beneficiary on the plan's designation form, which she never changed. Who receives the 401(k) account?
options: The son, because the will controls the disposition of all of the decedent's property
The son and the daughter equally, because the will and the designation conflict with each other
The daughter, because the designation form controls and the account passes outside the will
The estate, because a beneficiary designation is effective only if the will confirms it
items.rule_line: Assets with a named beneficiary, including retirement accounts and life insurance, pass by the designation and not by the will.

why.A: A will does not override a valid beneficiary designation on a retirement account.
why.B: There is no rule that splits conflicting instruments. The designation form governs the account.
why.C: Retirement accounts pass by beneficiary designation form and not through probate under the will.
why.D: The designation is effective on its own terms and does not need confirmation in the will.

guide.reveal: The beneficiary designation form on file with the plan.
